results.content: Published Time: 2002-01-01 (PDF) Sample design and estimation for household surveys Sample design and estimation for household surveys Download full-text PDFRead full-text Household surveys are a widely-used tool for obtaining information about a population of people. Traditional sample design and estimation methods ignore these dependencies.Methodologies which explicitly allow for the dependencies which may arise within households are developed in four areas: Estimating the design effects of standard estimators, for survey design; Constructing new estimators to exploit dependencies within households; Selecting a set of auxiliary variables to use in regression estimation; Allocating the sample sizes of households and of people within households.In each case, new methods will be developed which allow for the population structure of people within households. It is shown that, in estimating the variance at the sample design stage, the variation of household size must be considered. Existing criteria for selecting which auxiliary variables to use in regression estimation are extended to the case of two-stage sampling, and applied to household surveys. The fact that the number of people in a household is small leads to some novel and efficient sample designs and estimators. TWO-STAGE SAMPLE DESIGN WITH SMALL CLUSTERS In two-stage surveys, the sample size of clusters and units within clusters can be chosen to minimise the variance of an estimator, for fixed cost. We develop more flexible designs by optimizing survey cost, based on a simple cost model, subject to a required variance for an estimator of population total. The innovation lies in the fact that household sample sizes are small integers, which creates challenges in both design and estimation. results.title: A Two-Stage IPD Meta-Analysis Approach - ResearchGate
results.content: A Primer on Synthesizing Individual Participant Data Obtained From Complex Sampling Surveys:A Two-Stage IPD Meta-Analysis Approach Centre for Educational Measurement at the University of Oslo(CEMO),Faculty of Educational Sciences,University of Oslo Department of Psychology,Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences,National University of Singapore The increasing availability of individual p articipant data(IPD)in the social sciences offer s new possibilities to synthesize research evidence across primary studies.Two-stage IPD meta-analysis represents a framework that can utilize these possibilities.While most of the methodological resear ch on two-stage IPD meta-analysis focused on its performance compared with other approaches,dealing with the complexitie s of the primary and meta-analytic data has received little attention,particularly when IPD are drawn from complex sampling sur- veys.Complex sampling surveys often feature clustering,strati ﬁ cation,and multistage sampling to obtain nationally or internationally representative data from a target population.Furth ermore,IPD from these studies is likely to provide more than one effect size.To address these complexities,we propo se a two-stage meta- analytic approach that generates model-based effect sizes in Stage 1 and synthesizes them in Stage 2.We pres- ent a sequence of steps,illustrate their implement ation,and discuss the methodological decisions and options within.Given its ﬂ exibility to deal with the complex nature of the primary and meta-analytic data and its ability to combine multiple IPD sets or IPD with aggregated data,the proposed two-stage approach opens up new ana- lytic possibilities for synthesizing knowledge from complex sampling surveys. Meta-analyses are key tools to synthesize and accumulate evidence in psychological research.The increasing availability of data from individual participants shared by rese archers and institutions provides new opportuni- ties for meta-analyses.Some of the openly available data sets are based on complex sampli ng designs—that is, designs that typically involve multistage samplin g(e.g.,randomly sampling schools ﬁ rst and then students within schools),clustering(e.g.,students nested in schools),and strati ﬁ cation(e.g.,randomly sam pling students from different socioeconomic status groups).These designs pose metho dological challenges to the meta- analysis of individual participant data,not only when generating the effect sizes of interest but al so when syn- thesizing these effect sizes across primary studies or data sets.Speci ﬁ cally,both the analysis and synthesis of complex survey data need to consider the sample design features of the primary studies and the dependencies among effect sizes during the meta-analysis.This article presents a two-stage approach to synthesizing individ- ual participant data from complex sampling designs.We illustrate this approach with tw o meta-analytic exam- ples from educational psychology(i.e.,the negative effect of classroom achievement on students’self-concept in mathematics[big-ﬁ sh-little-pond-effect]and gender differences in secondary-school students’digital skills) and present hands-on steps.Researchers can ﬁ nd extensive online supplementary material to reproduce our results and translate the syntax to their research contexts.
